8.t: Working with data: comparing two proteins
q: Rank the species from most to least closely related to humans, using haemoglobin.
Gorilla, rhesus monkey, dog, kangaroo, frog.
Calculate the percentage of haemoglobin beta amino acids that differ in the frog.
Explain how these data support common ancestry.

All these species have the same proteins with similar sequences; the differences fit the expected order of relationship, as expected if mutations accumulated after lineages split from a common ancestor.
The two proteins rank the dog and the kangaroo differently. Suggest why.
Proteins change at different rates, and with small numbers of differences chance matters; many genes should be compared.
Explain why cytochrome c shows fewer differences than haemoglobin.
Cytochrome c is more conserved: almost any change harms the electron transport chain, so most mutations are removed by natural selection.
Suggest why DNA sequences give stronger evidence than protein sequences.
DNA includes silent mutations and non-coding regions, so there are many more differences to count.
Calculate the percentage change in mean hind-leg length on island B over 30 years.
Suggest how the vegetation on island B could cause this change by natural selection.

Leg length varies and is partly inherited. On thin branches, shorter-legged lizards are more agile, so they escape predators and catch food better, survive and reproduce more, and pass on their alleles.
Suggest an explanation that is not evolution, and how you could test it.
Legs may simply grow differently on thin perches (plasticity). Test: raise hatchlings from both islands in the same conditions and compare their legs.
The error bars for island B overlap at 20 and 30 years. State what this means.
The difference between those years may not be significant: it could be due to chance.
State what would show that the two populations had become separate species.
If they could no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring when brought together.
